title: JKH 2Q PBT up 2% to Rs. 7.95 b; attributable profit soars 213% | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:00
-     - 15

Chairperson Krishan Balendra

John Keells Holdings PLC (JKH) yesterday said profit attributable to equity holders of the parent rose 213% to Rs. 5.17 billion in the second quarter of 2026/27, from Rs. 1.65 billion a year earlier, while Group profit before tax (PBT) increased 2% to Rs. 7.95 billion from Rs. 7.8 billion.

Group profit after tax (PAT) of Rs. 5.82 billion was an increase of 39% over the Rs. 4.20 billion recorded in the corresponding quarter of the previous financial year. The company said the higher flow through to attributable PAT primarily reflected the lower effective contribution from John Keells CG Auto (JKCG), in which the Group has an ownership of 50%.

Group earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) of Rs. 18.30 billion in the quarter was broadly in line with the Rs. 18.36 billion recorded a year earlier. Growth across most industry groups offset the materially lower contribution from JKCG, against an exceptionally strong comparative quarter in the previous year, which benefited from pent-up demand following the resumption of vehicle imports. Cumulative Group EBITDA for the first half of 2026/27 increased by 11% to Rs. 34.65 billion.

The year-on-year PBT comparison was similarly impacted by the strong comparative base at JKCG. The appreciation of the Sri Lankan Rupee during the quarter also had a net impact of Rs. 340 million on Group PBT. Excluding the impact of net exchange movements, Group PBT was Rs. 7.61 billion, against Rs. 8.04 billion a year earlier.

Colombo West International Terminal (CWIT), the project company of West Container Terminal (WCT-1), maintained its strong operational momentum, handling 502,351 TEUs and operating beyond full utilisation of its phase 1 capacity. CWIT became the fastest terminal in the Port of Colombo to handle two million TEUs, reaching the milestone within 18 months of starting operations. Phase 2 operations have commenced with the progressive commissioning of equipment, and the terminal remains on track for full operations in December 2026.

The Transportation industry group recorded an increase in EBITDA driven by a very strong performance in the Group’s bunkering business, Lanka Marine Services (LMS), with volumes increasing by 31% together with higher margins, and a higher contribution from CWIT.

Profitability improved across the Beverages and Confectionery businesses, supported by volume growth of 10% in carbonated soft drinks and 7% in Confectionery, while the Convenience Foods business also recorded improved volumes and profitability.

The Supermarket business recorded 13% same store sales growth, supported by higher basket values and customer footfall. EBITDA increased marginally despite higher electricity and distribution costs, reflecting scale and operational efficiencies.

As anticipated, JKCG’s performance moderated against the exceptionally strong comparative quarter. JKCG handed over more than 2,400 vehicles during the quarter.

The Leisure industry group EBITDA reflected lower contributions from Colombo Hotels and Maldivian Resorts, including the impact of disruptions to travel from the conflict in the Middle East, partly offset by improved profitability across the Sri Lankan Resorts.

The ramp-up of City of Dreams Sri Lanka continued, with improving operating momentum across its key components. Higher occupancy and average room rates supported growth in hotel EBITDA, while the casino demonstrated an encouraging improvement in performance as operations progressively scaled up.

The Property industry group recorded EBITDA growth driven by profit recognition from residential and commercial unit sales at Cinnamon Life and residential sales at TRI-ZEN.

The Group’s share of profit after tax from Nations Trust Bank (NTB) increased, supported by a one-off tax credit arising from the acquisition of HSBC Sri Lanka’s retail banking business. This benefit was partly offset by integration expenses associated with onboarding the acquired business. Union Assurance (UA) recorded growth in gross written premiums, driven by renewal premiums.

JKH also noted that Fitch Ratings upgraded Sri Lanka’s sovereign credit rating to ‘B-’ from ‘CCC+’, which it described as a significant milestone reflecting the progress achieved in restoring macroeconomic stability.

While the Group’s carbon footprint and water withdrawal increased in absolute terms, operational intensity metrics across key businesses in the Consumer Foods, Leisure and Transportation industry groups, which account for the majority of the Group’s carbon footprint and water withdrawal, reflected improved efficiency.

The Board declared a first interim dividend of 10 cents per share, to be paid on or before 2 December, 2026.

title: Seylan Bank bullish on better growth on the back of strong foundation in recent years | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:33
-     - 8

Director and CEO Ramesh Jayasekera gestures during a media roundtable yesterday 

– Pic by Upul Abayasekara

By Nisthar Cassim

Seylan Bank yesterday expressed a bullish outlook for both Sri Lanka and the industry, hinting at much higher growth for the Bank on the strength of the foundation laid in recent years and achievements including surpassing the Rs. 1 trillion assets mark.

“There are a lot of positives in terms of the country’s macroeconomic fundamentals, and if interest rates remain as they are, and with 4% to 5% GDP growth and private sector resilience, we are bullish about 2027 as well as SMEs, retail business and private banking,” Seylan Bank Director and CEO Ramesh Jayasekera told 

the media. 

He singled out geopolitics and climate change as key risks for many countries, including Sri Lanka, but expressed confidence that, given inherent resilience, the growth momentum will continue.

Jayasekera said Seylan will explore both organic and inorganic opportunities for higher future growth.

Despite challenging conditions, over the past three and a half years the Bank has made significant progress in tandem with the foundation laid and pillars put in place for higher yet sustainable growth in the future.

Its asset base, from around Rs. 672 billion in 2023, crossed the Rs. 1 trillion mark in September this year, thereby making Seylan the fourth private commercial bank to reach the milestone.

“This is an important step in the Bank’s growth journey and reflects the confidence customers have placed in Seylan Bank. The milestone also reflects the contribution of employees and the Bank’s continued focus on meeting the financial needs of individuals and businesses. The achievement should be viewed not simply as a balance sheet figure, but as a reflection of the Bank’s expanding scale and customer relationships,” the Seylan Director/CEO said.

With SMEs accounting for 23% of its customer base, its lending portfolio grew by 25% in 2025 and is projected to achieve an 18% increase in 2026.

During the first nine months of 2026, loans and advances recorded net growth of Rs. 89 billion to Rs. 689 billion, and customer deposits increased by Rs. 78 billion to Rs. 811 billion.

Jayasekera revealed that over 50% of its 1.6 million customer base now does its banking digitally, as opposed to 16% in 2023, reflecting growing adoption. As a prudent strategy, provisioning for Stage 3 Non-Performing Loans has been increased to 85%, as against 54% in 2023. Seylan’s capital base is also strong, with Tier 1 at 11% and Tier 2 at 15%, whilst its Liquidity Coverage Ratio is at 170%. The Bank’s Stage 3 Impaired Loans Ratio stood at 1.02%, while its Total Capital Adequacy Ratio was 15.14%.

“With the foundation laid and pillars being put in place, and with the overall strength, we see greater capacity to grow better going forward,” Jayasekera said. After-tax profit, from Rs. 4.7 billion in 2023, reached Rs. 12 billion in 2025. In the first nine months of 2026, the figure was Rs. 9.1 billion, up 9.47% year-on-year.

Seylan in recent years has pursued an aggressive digital strategy, as evidenced by the growth in customers using mobile and internet banking. Loans on FDs, Pawning top-up, personal loans within 48 hours and decisions on new loans within 72 hours are some of its digitally enabled innovative products. The Bank aspires to provide a same-day leasing facility, whilst its foray into private banking is slated for early next year, with the first unit coming up at its head office in Colombo 3 and later in Colombo 7.

“We have been focusing on long-term relationship building as opposed to being a mere transactional bank,” explained Jayasekera in terms of customer success. He also stressed that SMEs are the DNA of Seylan and pointed to the multitude of long-standing and successful customers.

With a footprint of 170 branches and 3,300 employees countrywide, Seylan is also rolling out a new branch branding campaign, and will open two more branches in 2027, one each in the Jaffna District and Negombo.

As the business grows, Seylan said it is also reaching an important milestone in its ESG journey, completing 300 Pahasara school libraries across the country on 10th November. Pahasara has been a project that has reached over 700,000 children across the country over the past years, making reading, technology and learning more accessible and interesting.

title: Record Rs. 30 b  BOC debenture issue oversubscribed | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:26
-     - 8

Bank of Ceylon (BOC) yesterday said its debenture issue of up to Rs. 30 billion, the largest in Sri Lanka, had been oversubscribed, with applications exceeding 

Rs. 30 billion.

The State-owned bank initially offered up to 100 million debentures at an issue price of Rs. 100 each to raise up to Rs. 10 billion.

 It had the option to issue a further 100 million debentures to raise up to another Rs. 10 billion in the event of an oversubscription of the initial issue, and a further 100 million to raise up to a further Rs. 10 billion if both the initial issue and the second tranche were oversubscribed.

Accordingly, the issue was closed at 4.30 p.m. yesterday, as per the prospectus, the bank said. The basis of allotment will be notified to the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in due course.

The issue comprises Basel III-compliant Tier 2 listed, rated, unsecured, subordinated, redeemable debentures with five-year (2026/2031) and seven-year (2026/2033) tenures. Tier 2 capital is a supplementary layer of capital that counts towards a bank’s regulatory capital requirements. The debentures carry a non-viability write-down feature, which means they can be written down if the bank is deemed no longer viable, a standard requirement for such capital under Basel III rules.

The issue surpasses Commercial Bank of Ceylon’s Rs. 20 billion debenture issue in July 2024, which was billed at the time as the largest ever by a private bank.

title: SL fundamentals strong for frontier revival; Budget must focus on fiscal reforms momentum | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:22
-     - 8

Sri Lanka’s economy is on a strong footing on the back of fiscal discipline and significantly higher Government revenue, and is well placed to gain as frontier markets enter a new cycle of global investment, executives of Capital Alliance Holdings PLC (CAL) and Asia Frontier Capital Ltd., (AFC) said yesterday.

Speaking at a media briefing on CAL’s acquisition of a 51% stake in the Hong Kong-based fund manager, Group CEO Kanishke Mannakkara said the fiscal responsibility framework must continue through the upcoming Budget.

“The Government has made some very laudable efforts at widening the tax net, and the level of Government revenue in the country has increased very significantly,” he said.

Mannakkara called for a healthy primary surplus, a contained fiscal deficit and a shift from recurrent expenditure to capital investment, including through changes to procurement rules. With slightly more fiscal space, he said, the Government should consider moderating, rather than cutting, taxes to attract private investors.

“Right now in Sri Lanka, if you make 100 rupees of profit, by the time you pay your corporation tax and your dividend distribution tax, you pay 40%. It’s not 30%,” he said, noting that many countries set personal tax rates above corporate rates.

Mannakkara said Sri Lanka had strong momentum early this year before tensions in the Middle East hit prices, and that it and a few other frontier markets remained on course for significant growth that would restore investor confidence. “Of course, the big caveat is that things can change for the worse in the Middle East, and then all bets are off.”

AFC Fund Manager Ruchir Desai said Sri Lankan equities were down around 17% in US dollar terms this year, against about 1% for Pakistani stocks, and the Rupee had also weakened, but the sell-off looked overdone given the country’s economic position.

“The primary headwinds for Sri Lanka right now are external and geopolitical rather than structural domestic issues. Once tensions in the Middle East subside, I expect Sri Lanka and neighbouring regional markets to regain upward momentum,” Desai said.

He said the market would probably have posted solid gains this year had the war not occurred, as Sri Lanka had been recovering well since the 2022 crisis, with lower inflation and better political stability. Global geopolitics remained the main swing factor, he added. AFC’s own monthly updates attributed a 7.9% fall in its flagship fund in March 2026 to Middle East uncertainty that unsettled investors in Vietnam, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, followed by a 6.3% rebound in April after a ceasefire announcement.

Mannakkara said valuations were now near cyclical lows, and even in fixed income, higher interest rates meant lower entry prices for buyers. “Across the board, Sri Lankan assets have re-priced attractively, presenting viable opportunities across both equities and fixed income,” he said, cautioning that what looks attractive today could look different in six months, depending on where the economy sits in the cycle.

He said far more global capital had been allocated to frontier markets 12 to 14 years ago than today, as allocators exited the asset class. “These things do move in cycles, and we think this is probably the start of a cycle for frontier again.”

With global money flowing disproportionately into AI infrastructure, Mannakkara argued that frontier markets’ weak or negative correlation with the rest of the world made them a natural diversifier, and that their perceived risk exceeded actual risk for investors with a presence on the ground.

CAL Global Markets and Investment Banking Managing Director Deshan Pushparajah said global markets were volatile, driven largely by AI trades, while frontier economies rooted in real goods and resources offered international investors a counterbalance.

Desai said Sri Lanka was in a strong position and should maintain its momentum, noting that past Budgets had been marked by unstable tax policy. “Whether it’s this Budget or next year’s Budget, what matters is policy stability, to give investors confidence.”

AFC Founder and CEO Thomas Hugger said that while portfolio investment mattered, Sri Lanka needed foreign direct investment from multinationals and large corporations, and should use its strategic location to attract it. Citing Uzbekistan, where the current President opened the country, scrapped visa requirements for visitors and allowed investors to enter and exit freely, he said Sri Lanka must make it easy for foreign investors both to invest and to exit.

CAL’s wholly owned Singapore subsidiary CAL Global Pte. Ltd. signed a Share Purchase Agreement on 2 November, 2026 to acquire the 51% stake for approximately $ 2.5 million, subject to conditions precedent and regulatory approvals, including from Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission.

AFC managed approximately $ 125 million as at 30 September, 2026, through the multi-country AFC Asia Frontier Fund and dedicated funds for Vietnam, Uzbekistan and Iraq. 

The flagship fund invests in listed companies with their principal business in 20 Asian frontier markets where favourable demographics, rising incomes and high GDP growth are driving consumption: Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Georgia, Iraq, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Laos, the Maldives, Mongolia, Myanmar, Nepal, Oman, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Sri Lanka, Timor-Leste, Uzbekistan and Vietnam. 

According to AFC, its USD A-shares returned 27.1% in 2023, 23.1% in 2024, 19.7% in 2025 and 9.25% in the first nine months of 2026, while the AFC Iraq Fund returned 175.6% in the three years to March 2026.

Mannakkara said AFC had effectively doubled in size over the last four years, while CAL’s assets under management rose roughly 15 to 17 times over eight years to more than $ 1.2 billion across Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

He said the deal addressed the complexity that kept global capital away from markets such as Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Pakistan, as AFC already had the infrastructure for global investors to take positions in frontier markets easily. “Having the plumbing is useless if you don’t have the deals. AFC gives the plumbing.”

With Sri Lanka’s GDP at about $ 100 billion and Bangladesh’s just under $ 500 billion, Mannakkara said AFC’s three markets added a further $ 900 billion or so. At its initial public offering in April 2025, CAL set a target of serving economies with a combined GDP of over $ 1 trillion by 2030.

“Sri Lanka itself is too small to really be interesting for global capital. It’s by incorporating Sri Lanka into a bigger picture and a bigger story that you can really add value,” Mannakkara said.

Pushparajah said CAL’s presence in Bangladesh had already opened that market to Sri Lankan investors and companies, and AFC would take the group into Southeast, Central and West Asia, connecting frontier markets with one another.

title: LAUGFS Gas outlines Nov., shipment plans and measures to restore LPG supplies | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:02
-     - 11

LAUGFS Gas PLC yesterday said it has arranged three LPG shipments expected to arrive in Sri Lanka this month and is working with the relevant authorities to secure approvals for domestic supplies through its Hambantota terminal.

The company said it sincerely regrets the hardship caused to households and businesses by the current supply disruptions. “As a Sri Lankan company serving the domestic LPG market for more than 25 years, LAUGFS remains committed to restoring availability and strengthening long-term supply reliability,” it said.

Expected November shipments:

These dates remain subject to shipping arrangements, port operations and applicable regulatory approvals. Domestic releases from the Hambantota shipments require the necessary authorisations. Distribution is expected to resume progressively following receipt and clearance of the cargoes.

Supply challenges and the Hambantota terminal

Conflict in the Middle East and disruptions to maritime transport through the Strait of Hormuz have affected international LPG supply chains, creating procurement and shipping difficulties for Sri Lanka and other importing countries.

To strengthen Sri Lanka’s LPG supply security and support regional trade, LAUGFS Terminals Limited (LTL), a wholly owned subsidiary of LAUGFS Gas PLC, invested $ 65 million in its Hambantota import and export terminal, which commenced operations in 2019. With 30,000 metric tonnes of storage capacity, it is Sri Lanka’s largest LPG receiving, storage and entrepôt terminal.

The project received capital goods import-duty concessions under the Board of Investment’s Commercial Hub framework, subject to the applicable conditions. Under the relevant Hub Regulations, domestic releases are linked to 40% of annual re-export turnover by value. This is an export-linked operating condition, not a restriction on LAUGFS Gas’s domestic market share.

The COVID-19 pandemic, Sri Lanka’s economic and political crisis, foreign-exchange shortages and sovereign credit-rating downgrades disrupted LTL’s ability to maintain the required re-export levels. The resulting regulatory restrictions have limited the terminal’s availability for domestic supply despite its substantial storage capacity.

Temporary permission previously granted by the Finance Ministry under Emergency Regulations ceased when those regulations ended.

Steps to enable domestic supply

LTL has requested three months of temporary permission to use the Hambantota terminal for domestic LPG supply. In parallel, the company is working with the BOI, Finance Ministry, Sri Lanka Customs and the Department of Imports and Exports Control to complete its transition out of hub status and establish the necessary operating arrangements, with applicable duties and taxes payable.

The BOI Chairman confirmed to the company yesterday that, following instructions from the President, he had written to the Treasury Secretary requesting that the necessary approvals be facilitated within one week. These approvals remain pending. LAUGFS appreciates the Government’s intervention and the cooperation of the relevant authorities.

As an additional supply safeguard, LAUGFS Gas has also called a new tender for direct LPG deliveries to Colombo commencing in January 2027.

Clarification on OFAC designation

LAUGFS Gas PLC and LAUGFS Terminals Ltd., are not itself entities designated by the US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Asset Control (OFAC). The company remains committed to applicable regulatory and compliance requirements and to maintaining transparency with its stakeholders.

LAUGFS Gas PLC appreciates its customers and business partners for their patience and will provide further updates as shipment arrivals and regulatory approvals are confirmed, the company said.

title: New Asia Forum 2026 targets $ 30 b in  investment mobilisation | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:00
-     - 8

The New Asia Forum (NAF) 2026 aims to mobilise $ 30 billion in investment across the New Asia region by strengthening strategic partnerships and accelerating investment execution. 

Held under the patronage of President Prabowo Subianto, with Danantara Indonesia as a founding partner, the forum will take place on 3–4 December 2026 in Bali, Indonesia.

NAF 2026 is designed as an action-oriented platform connecting global investors, industry leaders, and policymakers to advance investment opportunities across strategic sectors. Moving beyond conventional economic dialogue, the forum seeks to translate investment interest into concrete commitments, financing structures, and measurable outcomes.

Danantara Indonesia, Global Relations and Communications Managing Director Pahala Nugraha Mansury emphasised Asia’s growing potential to attract long-term global capital amid shifting economic and geopolitical dynamics.

“Our focus is on encouraging long-term capital to recognise the many investment opportunities across Asian countries, because this is precisely where the centre of gravity for growth lies. This will enable growth at scale, anchored by ASEAN and driven by Indonesia as the largest country in ASEAN,” said Pahala.

The Asia-Pacific region currently accounts for nearly 60% of global economic growth. However, long-term international capital allocation to the region remains below its potential, presenting significant opportunities for greater investment collaboration.

NAF 2026 expects to convene more than 1,000 global leaders, feature over 100 speakers, and host more than 40 sessions involving sovereign wealth funds, institutional investors, development finance institutions, multinational corporations, and government representatives. Notable speakers include President Prabowo Subianto of Indonesia; Masayoshi Son, Chairman and CEO of SoftBank Group; Tshering Tobgay, Prime Minister of Bhutan; Kathleen Quirk, Chief Executive Officer of Freeport-McMoRan; Matteo Renzi, former Prime Minister of Italy; and Israfil Mammadov, Chief Executive Officer of the State Oil Fund of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

The forum will follow a two-day structure: Discovery and Diligence on 3 December, focusing on investment opportunities, feasibility, and transaction structures; and Action and Execution on 4 December, advancing capital commitments, strategic partnerships, and implementation milestones.

Eight priority sectors will anchor the discussions: strategic resources and downstreaming; energy and power; advanced mobility and manufacturing; digital infrastructure and AI; food and agribusiness; trade and connectivity; tourism and creative economy; and education and human capital.

As a founding partner, Danantara Indonesia will participate as a co-investor alongside global partners, supporting investment in strategic sectors and reinforcing Indonesia’s role in regional economic transformation.

Through its transaction-focused approach, NAF 2026 aims to deliver preliminary investment agreements, bankable financing structures, and clearly defined implementation milestones. Investment commitments and progress will be tracked across subsequent editions to promote accountability, continuity, and tangible economic impact for Indonesia and the wider region.

title: Tension in House over no-confidence motion against Speaker | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:05
-     - 9

Parliament saw tense scenes yesterday after Deputy Speaker Rizvie Salih refused to immediately allow several privilege issues to be raised, including the Opposition’s no-confidence motion against Speaker Jagath Wickramaratne.

Salih told the House he had received copies of privilege issues submitted by several MPs after 9.00 a.m. He said he could not permit them to be raised until he had examined the submissions.

Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa said the refusal to take up the motion violated parliamentary privileges and democratic principles. The motion contains 50 charges against Speaker Wickramaratne and is signed by 44 Opposition MPs. According to Premadasa, it was handed to the Secretary-General of Parliament on 9 October, 2026 and included in Parliament’s Order Book on 12 October, 2026. It was later rejected following a decision by the Committee on Parliamentary Business, which denied the Opposition an opportunity to debate the allegations.

Premadasa argued that blocking the debate raised serious concerns over the Speaker’s impartiality, the independence of Parliament and the democratic rights of Opposition MPs. He also claimed restrictions were being imposed on freedom of speech, expression and debate in the House. He stressed that the Speaker was constitutionally obligated to act impartially and to give both Government and Opposition MPs fair opportunities to exercise their parliamentary rights. He called for an investigation into whether the refusal constituted a breach of parliamentary privileges.

Opposition MPs continued to object, which led to a tense exchange on the floor. Salih assured the House that the privilege issues would be examined and a response provided during the day. The Opposition kept up its protest, however, as the Government proceeded with scheduled business.

summary:

title: New UN Women report calls for stronger action to advance women’s political leadership in SL | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:00
-     - 6

UN Women Head of Office Ramaaya Salgado (right) presents the “Beyond Numbers” report to Mass Media Deputy Minister

Dr. Kaushalya Ariyarathne

UN Women yesterday launched a new report “Beyond Numbers” examining the impact and lessons of Sri Lanka’s 25% local government quota, bringing together government representatives, political actors, women leaders, civil society, development partners and the United Nations to discuss the future of women’s political participation and leadership in Sri Lanka.

Launched at a strategic dialogue convened by UN Women Sri Lanka, the report brought together government representatives, political actors, women leaders, civil society, development partners, academia and the United Nations to reflect on the future of women’s political participation and leadership in Sri Lanka.

The launch comes at an important moment for the country. Recent elections have brought notable gains in women’s representation and visibility in political office, including an increase in the number of women elected to Parliament. While these developments signal progress, women continue to face barriers at multiple stages of political participation, including party gatekeeping, limited access to campaign resources and political networks, unequal opportunities for leadership within party structures, harassment and violence, and persistent social norms that question women’s legitimacy as political leaders.

The report highlights the significance of the 25% quota for women’s seats in local government, which increased women’s representation in local authorities from approximately 2% to nearly 23%. Beyond increasing numbers, the quota provides important lessons on what enables women to enter political institutions, the extent to which greater representation translates into influence, and where structural barriers continue to impede women’s leadership and participation.

UN Women Sri Lanka Head of Office Ramaaya Salgado said: “While increasing representation is important, the next challenge is ensuring that representation translates into meaningful participation, influence and leadership. The experiences of women who entered local government through the quota offer valuable insights into what works, what continues to limit women’s political participation, and what reforms are needed to create a more inclusive political landscape.”

Discussions during the dialogue explored the relationship between representation, influence and political leadership; the implications of the quota experience for future reforms at provincial and national levels; and the institutional, political and social changes needed to strengthen pathways for women’s leadership. Participants also examined issues related to nomination processes, campaign financing, leadership progression, safety, accountability and the broader enabling environment for women in politics.

The dialogue further underscored the importance of ensuring that efforts to strengthen political participation are inclusive and responsive to the experiences of women facing multiple and intersecting forms of exclusion, including women from minority communities, women with disabilities, young women, rural women, women affected by conflict, and women outside established political networks.

The event forms part of UN Women’s ongoing support to evidence-based policymaking, inclusive governance and women’s leadership in Sri Lanka. Findings from the report and recommendations emerging from the dialogue will contribute to future policy engagement, advocacy, programming and partnerships aimed at advancing women’s political participation and leadership, and ensuring that increased representation translates into meaningful influence and lasting change.

This version reads more like a media story because it starts with the announcement, explains why it matters now, then moves into the findings and stakeholder discussion.

Full report is available at https://bit.ly/women-local-governance

title: The State must keep time, too | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:22
-     - 0

The scaling back of Port City tax concessions after investors had committed did more damage than any single failed project, because it showed that even our flagship stability zone could alter its own terms

Every Sri Lankan knows the feeling. A tax return is due by a fixed date, and a day’s delay brings a penalty. An appeal must be lodged within a set number of days, or the right to it is lost. A licence lapses at midnight; a renewal fee is surcharged the morning after. The citizen and the business live by the calendar, and the law enforces it without sentiment. 

Now consider the other side of the counter. An application for an approval is submitted, and then nothing. There is no date by which the State must answer, no consequence if it does not, and frequently no one who can say where the file is. The citizen is on the clock; the State is not. That asymmetry is not a minor administrative irritation. It is, I would argue, one of the principal reasons Sri Lanka’s hard-won economic recovery has not yet turned into the investment the country needs.

A recovery that has not yet become investment

Let us give credit where it is due. Foreign direct investment (FDI) reached approximately $1.06 billion in 2025, the first time inflows have crossed the billion-dollar mark, and a rise of roughly 72% on 2024. Revenue collection has been restored. The Public Debt Management Act, No. 33 of 2024, has placed debt reporting on a transparent statutory footing. Our position on the corruption perceptions ranking improved from 121st to 107th in a single year. These are real achievements, and they belong to the country, not to any one party.

Yet the numbers that matter most remain stubborn. FDI is still close to 1% of GDP. The 2025 target of $ 5 billion was met at about one fifth. Most individual transactions sit in the $ 3 to 5 million range. And South Asian FDI as a whole grew by 35% in 2025, which means we are riding a regional tide rather than outperforming our neighbours. The sovereign rating stands at CCC+.

The clock runs against the recipient, never against the State

Consider what the mid-sized investor, the person who actually makes up most of our transactions, encounters on arrival. To open an Inward Investment Account (IIA), through which capital must legally enter the country, original physical documents must be couriered or hand-delivered from abroad. There is no uniform procedure across licensed banks, with each institution applying its own internal processes. More importantly, the Central Bank has not published prescribed guidelines setting out the mandatory disclosures required from investors or specifying maximum processing timelines. Consequently, while the investor is bound by strict compliance requirements, neither the banks nor the regulator is subject to a corresponding standard of procedural certainty or timeliness. Unless the Central Bank addresses these gaps by introducing uniform procedures, clear disclosure requirements and prescribed processing timelines, the framework remains deficient in both prudence and substance.

The expatriate work authorisation process is starker still. A foreign hire needs a sponsoring body recommendation, then an entry visa, then conversion to a residence visa after arrival. If that person leaves the country within the one-month entry visa window, the process
starts again. The applicant has a month. The three agencies involved have no deadline at all. The time limits have caused significant difficulties in both attracting and maintaining Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). I can think of no better illustration of a system that measures the citizen’s time precisely and the State’s time not at all.

The same pattern runs through the courts. A litigant who misses a prescribed period may lose a case before it is heard. Meanwhile 1.13 million cases are pending across 293 courts. The rules of procedure are strict with the party and silent on the delay. Contract enforcement is now slow enough that every investor prices it into every deal, and we pay that premium, whether or not we ever see the dispute.

No approval in our investment framework carries a legislated deadline. The Board of Investment (BOI) functions as a nominal single window, while real decision-making authority is spread across several ministries, the Central Environmental Authority, the water and electricity boards and local authorities. Investors report approaching municipal councils and ministries separately for a single project. Each agency is entitled to take its time; none is obliged to explain it. When everyone holds a veto and no one holds a deadline, delay is not a failure of the system. It is the system. Sri Lanka’s continued rhetoric on investment facilitation must be translated into urgent legislative and administrative action; otherwise, it will remain mere rhetoric.

Why this matters more than incentives

We have spent decades debating tax holidays and concessions. But the marginal investor in Sri Lanka is not a multinational deciding between continents; it is a firm placing a few million dollars and borrowing against a construction schedule. For an investor, an approval that may take three months or eighteen months is not merely an inconvenience; it is an unfinanceable risk. Predictability of process matters more than the generosity of the incentive, just as, in labour law, predictability of cost matters more than the level of cost. That is precisely why the absence of prescribed timelines in any of our guidelines or handbooks cannot be justified: the framework must provide foreign investors with a predictable timeframe within which approvals will be processed.

There is also a question of fairness that goes beyond economics. A State that demands punctuality from its people while exempting itself teaches a corrosive lesson: that rules are for the governed, not for those who govern. Investors notice that. So do our own
professionals: skilled workers now account for 76.5% of departures for foreign employment. We are losing the very educated workforce we advertise.

From stability to growth: why investors are the test

Sri Lanka has spent the years since the crisis doing the hard and necessary work of stabilisation: restoring revenue, restructuring debt and rebuilding the credibility of our public finances. Stability, however, is a floor, not a destination. The task now is to convert it into growth, and growth on the scale we need cannot be financed by the State alone. With the sovereign rating at CCC+, commercial borrowing markets remain effectively closed to us. Domestic savings are rebuilding slowly. Foreign direct investment is therefore not one option among many; it is the principal source of the capital, technology and market access that will determine whether the recovery becomes durable.

FDI also has a quality that borrowed money does not. It does not have to be repaid on a fixed schedule, it brings skills and export markets with it, and it creates the jobs that may persuade our professionals to build their careers at home. As heavy debt service resumes in 2028, a country that has diversified its sources of capital will face those repayments from strength. A country that has not will be tempted back into the same cycle that brought us to crisis.

The Government must give greater credence to attracting foreign direct investment, improving Sri Lanka’s competitiveness as an investment destination and establishing a predictable, prudent and investor-friendly tax policy. Revenue mobilisation is important, but it cannot be the sole measure of economic success. 

This is precisely why the timeliness of the State matters so much. Investors do not compare Sri Lanka with its own past; they compare it with Thailand, Vietnam, and Malaysia, each competing for the same capital. Those jurisdictions offer investors something we too often do not: certainty about how long the State will take to say yes or no. Every month an approval sits unanswered is a month of financing costs, a delayed construction start and, increasingly, a decision to invest elsewhere. Investors can price risk; what they cannot price is silence.

The ambition is achievable. A credible path would lift FDI from about $ 1.06 billion today to $ 2.5 billion by 2028 and $ 4 billion by 2030, raising it from roughly 1% of GDP towards 3%. Those targets will not be met by promotional roadshows or fresh incentive packages. They will be met by making Sri Lanka the place where a project approved on a given date starts on a predictable one. Tellingly, the median time from application to construction start is not even measured today. What a government does not measure, it cannot manage, and what it cannot manage, investors will not trust.

Our natural advantages are real: a location on the main east-west shipping lanes, an extraordinary tourism endowment and a literate population that could make us a regional centre for higher education. But advantages that cannot be unlocked on time are advantages in name only. A State that answers promptly is the bridge between stability and growth.

Unless we are able to address the existing tax structure, Sri Lanka may no longer be a cost-competitive destination when labour costs are considered alongside the prevailing tax burden. Countries such as India and Bangladesh benefit from relatively lower labour costs, partly due to their large labour force and population. Consequently, when both taxation and labour costs are taken into account, Sri Lanka may no longer offer a significant cost advantage.

Put the State on the clock

The remedy is neither complicated nor expensive, and most of it requires no new Act of Parliament.


First, gazette maximum determination periods for every category of investment approval, and attach a rule of deemed approval: if an agency fails to respond within the period, the application is approved unless refused in writing with reasons. A published timeline without consequence is an aspiration. Deemed approval turns it into a commitment. This can be done by regulation under existing investment law within six months.

Second, the Central Bank should direct licensed banks to accept a single standard document set, certified digital submissions and electronic verification for the IIA, with a published maximum processing time. It is the cheapest reform available, and it sits at the very first step of the investor’s journey.

Third, consolidate expatriate work authorisation into a single permit issued through the BOI Visa Management System and accepted by the Department of Immigration and Emigration, extend the conversion window to six months, and permit conversion after travel. If the citizen’s window is to be generous, let it at least be as generous as the State’s.

Fourth, assign every approved project a named senior officer with authority to convene the agencies involved and a duty to report delays each month. Accountability needs a name, not merely an institution.

Fifth, publish a live project tracker showing every approved project above a defined threshold, its approval date, its current stage, the responsible agency and the reason for any delay. It will be uncomfortable for a quarter. After that it will be self-correcting, because no agency wishes to be named as the cause of delay.

Sixth, complete the Single Window for Investment, for which the Finance Ministry has already called proposals, and make it genuine: one interface and one status tracker covering BOI registration, incorporation, tax registration, environmental clearance, local authority approval and utility connections. A portal that merely forwards applications into the same silences would be worse than none.

And in the courts, fund the instrument we already have. The Mediation in Civil and Commercial Disputes Act, No. 13 of 2026, in force since 30 June, makes mediated settlements binding and enforceable and allows judges to refer suitable matters to mediation. International experience suggests settlement rates of 65 to 70%. What is missing is capacity and funding, not law, together with published disposal-time targets for labour tribunals and commercial mediation.

Beyond the next election

Timelines alone will not suffice if the rules themselves can change mid-stream. The scaling back of Port City tax concessions after investors had committed did more damage than any single failed project, because it showed that even our flagship stability zone could alter its own terms. A Cabinet policy statement grandfathering agreed terms, written into the standard BOI agreement, would cost nothing. Neither would a cross-party investment compact committing the principal parties to leave the core framework intact for at least ten years. FDI decisions run on twenty- to thirty-year horizons; ours have rarely survived a change of government.

This is not a partisan argument. On this question, there should be no sides. Much of the work has already been done: the labour law consolidation has been drafted and agreed at committee, the mediation law is in force, and the single window is in procurement. The scarce resource is not analysis. It is the will to bind the State to the same discipline it has always required of its citizens.

A country that respects its people’s time will find that investors respect it too. Let us put the State on the clock.

(The author is a President’s Counsel and a former Cabinet Minister)

title: Sri Lanka’s service crisis: When poor service becomes an economic problem | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:20
-     - 4

Sri Lankan hospitality was once unmatched. Warmth, attentiveness, and generosity were qualities associated not only with our tourism industry but with the country itself. Increasingly, however, the experience of service in Sri Lanka tells a different story.

Across restaurants, retail, hospitality and even professional services, poor service is becoming difficult to ignore. Long waits, indifferent attitudes, limited product knowledge, poor communication and an apparent reluctance to go beyond the minimum are increasingly commonplace. While it is tempting to dismiss this as an “attitude problem”, doing so overlooks a more important question: what has happened to the environment in which Sri Lankans work?

A workforce under pressure

Sri Lanka has undergone an extraordinary succession of shocks: decades of conflict, the Easter attacks, COVID-19 and, most recently, the 2022 economic crisis. These experiences do not disappear simply because inflation stabilises or GDP begins growing again.

Perhaps, therefore, some of what we interpret as apathy is exhaustion.

There is an underlying pessimism that appears to have settled across parts of society. When employees feel financially insecure, see limited possibilities for advancement, and watch peers leave for opportunities overseas — expecting consistently enthusiastic service without addressing these underlying conditions is unrealistic.

The incentive problem

However, hardship cannot not explain poor service.


Service improves when there are incentives to provide it. Competitive markets create consequences and where competition is limited, employment is disconnected from performance. Organisations tolerate mediocrity and these incentives weaken. 

Low wages compound the problem. Employees cannot indefinitely be expected to deliver international standards while receiving remuneration that offers little economic security or incentive for excellence. Better service must therefore be accompanied by reasonable remuneration, recognition, career progression, and professionalisation of service occupations.

These are also questions of corporate governance. How businesses manage performance, reward employees and invest in human capital ultimately determines their productivity and competitiveness. Strong governance requires accountability at every level, including management’s responsibility to create the conditions in which employees can perform.

A skills and exposure gap

Sri Lanka’s skills problem predates the economic crisis. Much of the country’s workforce was historically shaped by a colonial education and employment system designed to produce disciplined administrators and service workers who could meet established standards – rather than innovators and independent problem-solvers. That model may once have served the needs of the British administration and the economy of its time, but it is increasingly outdated in a world that demands creativity, initiative, and adaptability. An education system that has changed too slowly, combined with institutional cultures shaped by hierarchy, entitlement and limited competition, has allowed these habits to become deeply embedded.

There is also a more fundamental question: do employees know what excellent service looks like? Customer service is itself a skill. Anticipating needs, communicating professionally, resolving complaints, understanding products and creating an experience require training and exposure. Businesses cannot demand “better attitudes” without investing in developing them.

Should Sri Lanka import labour?

Sri Lanka may also need to confront a politically uncomfortable question: does the country have enough people willing and able to fill the jobs its economy requires?

As Sri Lankans migrate for higher wages while certain domestic industries struggle to recruit and retain workers, carefully regulated inward labour migration deserves serious consideration. Sri Lanka is already experiencing labour and skills shortages in sectors including agriculture and construction, prompting growing discussion around regional labour mobility.

Foreign labour should not substitute for improving wages and conditions for Sri Lankan workers. However, selective labour migration could alleviate genuine shortages, introduce new skills and, importantly, increase competition within parts of the labour market.

Service is an economic asset

Sri Lanka increasingly depends on services to generate employment, tourism receipts, investment and economic growth. The World Bank identifies tourism and services as important contributors to the country’s recent recovery. A country seeking higher-value tourists and foreign investment cannot accept declining service standards as inevitable.

The experience of Singapore demonstrates what sustained investment in service quality, skills and institutional standards can achieve. Over the past decade, Singapore has continued to strengthen its position as a global services hub, particularly in finance, logistics, professional services, tourism and digital industries. Singapore’s progress has not been based simply on demanding better attitudes from workers. It has involved systematic investment in education, technical and vocational training, productivity, digitalisation and service standards, supported by institutions such as SkillsFuture and the Singapore Tourism Board.

India offers a different but equally relevant example. Its services sector has expanded rapidly over the past decade and now account for more than half of India’s economic output. This growth has been supported by a large pool of technically trained workers, expanding digital infrastructure, English-language capability, private-sector competition and deliberate efforts to improve skills and employability.

Neither example is directly transferable to Sri Lanka. Singapore has far greater fiscal capacity and a highly centralised system, while India benefits from a much larger domestic market and a substantial technology workforce. But both demonstrate that service quality and service-sector growth are not accidental. They emerge when countries combine skills development, competition, infrastructure, professional management, technology, and credible standards.

Conclusion: Invest in people

The solution therefore requires action from both Government and business: modernise vocational and soft-skills education; professionalise service careers; reward excellence; facilitate carefully regulated foreign labour where genuine shortages exist; and create more competitive markets in which consumers can hold businesses accountable.

Most importantly, businesses must invest again in their people. This is where the social dimension of ESG becomes particularly relevant. Fair remuneration, employee well-being, skills development and opportunities for advancement are fundamental to building a productive and motivated workforce. Service quality cannot sustainably exceed the quality of the employment experience behind it.

Sri Lanka’s service problem may ultimately be telling us something larger about the country’s recovery. Rebuilding an economy requires more than restoring reserves, reducing inflation, or increasing GDP. It demands greater investment in human capital, responsible business practices, and the social foundations of long-term economic resilience. Above all, it is about restoring aspiration — empowering people with the skills, incentives, exposure and belief that doing something well is worth the effort.

title: Why Sri Lanka needs serious reset of its tourism strategy | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:00
-     - 5

TWC Holdings Chairman Thilan Wijesinghe speaks at the THINC Tourism Conference

Following is the speech by TWC Holdings Chairman Thilan Wijesinghe on the subject ‘Tourism Uncensored’ at the THINC Tourism Conference on 15 October, 2026. Drawing on 20 years in small luxury tourism, starting with Ceylon Tea Trails, Wijesinghe, who is also a Director of Ventive Hospitality (India), Resplendent Ceylon and Tea Trails, sets out what Sri Lanka got right and wrong in tourism. He faults successive governments for arrival targets without strategy, mispriced State land and lax coastal zoning, and calls for a strategic reset through five policy reforms and two ‘moonshot’ projects to move the country up the tourism value chain.

As the subject assigned to me is Tourism Uncensored, I intend to speak candidly about the lessons I have learnt over the past 20 years while pursuing my passion for small luxury tourism in Sri Lanka. I will speak also about what we got right, what we got wrong, and what I believe we must do differently if Sri Lanka is to realise its tourism potential.

In 2004, I undertook a seven-day road trip around Sri Lanka with Robert Hecker, the Managing Director of Horwath, a well-known hotel consultancy firm. During that journey, I realised that Sri Lanka had received what may be one of the greatest destination taglines in history as far back as 1293, when Marco Polo described it as “the finest island of its size in the world”.


My own journey into small luxury tourism began in 2003, during a conversation with my friend and mentor, Nick Clayton, an Englishman whose father had been a tea planter in Malaysia. We had both spent our childhood holidays in plantation bungalows. We then conceived the idea of converting Sri Lanka’s old tea plantation bungalows into a small luxury resort, connected by walking trails. We presented the concept to the founders of Dilmah Tea, who became majority partners in the venture. That was the beginning of Ceylon Tea Trails.

What made the concept unique was that we did not need to build a conventional resort on one large, contiguous piece of land. Instead, we restored five plantation bungalows spread across an area of approximately 50 square kilometres and operate them as one integrated resort. We developed what we called a mothership-and-satellite concept: several individual properties, each with its own identity, brought together under one hospitality operation.

Lesson One: Power of global public relations

When Tea Trails opened in stages in 2006 and 2007, we encountered what I can only describe as a perfect storm. First, through my own naivety and inexperience, I had not estimated a pre-opening and marketing budget. Second, Sri Lanka’s conflict intensified during 2006 and 2007, creating an extremely difficult environment in which to launch a luxury tourism product.

Our saving grace came from an unexpected source. In 2006, the tourist board had entered into a public-relations contract with Batey, the Singapore-based PR agency known for its work on major tourism and the “Singapore Girl” campaigns.

I approached the then Chairman of the Tourist Board and requested permission to invite foreign journalists visiting Sri Lanka through this programme to experience Tea Trails. The resulting articles by these journalists were extraordinarily positive. International publications featured the resort as “The world’s best place to pop the question to your partner”, “Top five colonial holidays in the world”, “Best all-inclusive hotel in the world” and “The top 10 world's greatest trips”. 

Through strategic PR, Tea Trails became an aspirational destination overriding the negative country perception at the time. We were subsequently able to command higher room rates and build a profitable business.

The lesson is simple: strategic marketing and public relations are investments in enhancing the economic value of a tourism product or destination. The Government must therefore recognise that there is a substantial cost to not investing in strategic destination marketing.

Lesson Two: Design and storytelling determine what a resort can charge

My second lesson came soon after the end of the conflict. Around 2010, I became a shareholder in a 100-acre property on Sri Lanka’s East Coast. 

I asked the CEO of a prominent ground-handling company a straightforward question: “If I were to build a hotel here, what room rate could I expect?” His answer was that we might achieve between $ 80 and $ 100 per night. I then showed him photographs of a resort in Indonesia named Nihi Watu, in a remote location that was difficult to access. The resort’s design and concept offered a very different experience from a conventional beach hotel. When he saw the photographs, his assessment changed immediately. He believed that a resort of this nature could potentially command $ 200 to $ 250 per night.

That was a dramatic increase in the potential room rate, without relying simply on the location or the amount of money spent on construction. This conversation taught me something fundamental: the value of a resort is not determined by its location alone, nor by how much it costs to build. It is determined by the experience it offers, how distinctively it is designed, and how compellingly that experience is communicated to the market.

Lesson Three: Building hotels is not the same as building a destination

My third lesson came from Pasikuda on the East Coast. Following the end of the conflict, the Government invested in infrastructure, including roads, electricity and water, to encourage private investment in hotels. 

However, what emerged was a cluster of hotels ranging from five-star to two-star properties, without a coherent approach to destination planning, design, positioning or the overall visitor experience. There was little sense of place and limited coordination between the individual developments. Today, some properties in Pasikuda face serious financial difficulties, and others have reportedly been offered for sale, some at distressed prices.

Pasikuda was another lesson learnt: Sri Lanka has followed the simplistic assumption that if we build enough hotels, the tourists will come without always asking whether the product being built is appropriate for its location, whether it has a clear market position, and whether the destination as a whole will be competitive

Policy mistake: Targets without a credible strategy

In 2009, soon after the conflict ended the then President announced an ambitious target of attracting 3 million tourists by 2015. The Tourist Board then began to calculate the required number of rooms, divide the gap by the number of years remaining, and then approve construction accordingly. Successive governments have made the mistake of announcing arrival targets. This is not a tourism strategy.

Policy mistake: Mispricing scarce land

Another problem was the approach to pricing land for tourism development. In 2012, when my partners were acquiring freehold land on the East Coast at approximately Rs. 5.5 million per acre, the Government was quoting approximately Rs. 20 million per acre for 99-year leases on comparable East Coast lands – an almost 400% premium to the value of freehold land at the time! 

This matters particularly in Sri Lanka, where the State owns a substantial share of the land. Beachfront land suitable for tourism is a scarce economic resource. Government owned land should be allocated and priced in a manner that encourages the highest sustainable economic value from its use. When land is priced beyond what a high-quality resort can economically support, investors respond by reducing their development footprint, compromising the concept, or abandoning the investment altogether.

Policy mistake: Doing away with height restriction on beach properties

Another concern was the relaxation of height restrictions that had traditionally limited construction in coastal areas to the height of a coconut tree. Sri Lanka subsequently saw the growth of apartment developments on beachfront properties, marketed for short-term tourist accommodation.

In an island such as Sri Lanka, beachfront land is finite since we have issues with land title, roads and railways hugging the beach preventing tourism development, and in certain areas having inadequate utility infrastructure. If land suitable for a distinctive luxury resort is instead absorbed by developments that do not fit the area’s intended positioning, the opportunity to create a higher-value tourism product would be lost. This is particularly relevant to places such as Tangalle and Talpe, which have developed reputations for distinctive, low-density and high-end hospitality.

The Government’s responsibility is not simply to permit any construction. It is to ensure that development decisions collectively strengthen the destination through proper zoning laws.

The opportunity Sri Lanka has yet to capture

Such poor policy choices help explain why I believe Sri Lanka has not moved up the tourism value chain. More than 20 years ago, the Maldives attracted international luxury resort investments, at times costing USD 1 million per key, capable of commanding very high rates. Properties associated with brands such as One&Only, Cheval Blanc and Four Seasons helped establish the Maldives’ reputation in the luxury market.

Local brands such as Per Aquum evolved by piggy-backing on high-end international brands. While Sri Lanka has well-established local hospitality brands, we should ask why the country has not attracted a larger portfolio of internationally branded resorts, particularly at the upper end of the market. 

Only around 6% of Sri Lanka’s graded resort hotel rooms are internationally branded compared to at least 33% in tourism focused countries in Asia such as Maldives, Vietnam and Mauritius.

The value of international brands

International brands can bring distribution networks, loyalty programmes, global marketing, operating systems and access to customers who might otherwise not consider a destination. They can also help local investors benchmark their products against international standards.

Let me illustrate the point with an example. In March this year, before the escalation of the Middle East crisis, I enquired about booking eight rooms at Anantara Peace Haven Tangalle. I was quoted approximately $ 600 per night for a 55-square-metre room and $ 1,300 for a villa. Similarly, properties such as the Marriott Weligama and Hilton Yala outperform most local brands in terms of rates and occupancy.

Sri Lanka’s tourism earnings have not consistently reflected the extraordinary potential of its natural and cultural assets. We need to understand why, and then address the underlying causes. The strategic question remains: are we doing enough to attract investors and operators capable of helping us compete in the world’s most valuable tourism segments?

What should we do differently?

So, where do we go from here? My answer is that we need to reflect, reassess and re-strategise. Let me emphasise that strategy does not mean commissioning yet another master plan, of which there are many. The issue is whether our plans have been translated into coherent policies, investment decisions and measurable results.

Here are five “uncensored” proposals I would like to propose.

(1)Introduce destination-level zoning that determines what we want each tourism area to become. We should not repeat on the East Coast the mistakes that have occurred in many parts of the South Coast.

(2)Introduce viability-gap funding for domestic aviation. I have been advocating this for several years, particularly in relation to facilitating access to the North and East.

(3)Address the underutilisation of scarce beachfront land. This is perhaps my most controversial proposal. We should consider a carefully designed land tax or other fiscal mechanism for suitable beachfront land that remains undeveloped for extended periods. The objective should be to discourage speculative landholding that prevents productive use of a scarce resource.

(4)Restrict high-rise beachfront apartment developments to designated zones. High-rise developments may be appropriate in selected urban zones. It is not necessarily appropriate everywhere along our coastline. 

(5)Facilitate the repositioning of ageing hotels. Some of Sri Lanka’s established hotels occupy valuable sites but require substantial reinvestment to remain competitive. They should be encouraged to enter into joint ventures and rebranded, ideally involving international operators. Where aging and underperforming properties occupy State land, they must be encouraged to be repositioned with new investments.

Pursue moonshot projects

Beyond these reforms, I believe Sri Lanka needs to think bigger. We should identify one or two ambitious projects capable of changing how the world perceives the country. I have personally explored two such possibilities.

1.An internationally branded luxury train. Imagine attracting an internationally recognised luxury rail operator, potentially a brand such as Orient Express, to develop a world-class train experience in Sri Lanka. The Colombo-Badulla rail track is possibly one of the world’s most picturesque train journeys rising up to over 6000 feet above sea level and is the highest track in the world in the 5½ foot gauge. We are also probably the only country in the world where in under a day you can take a train to all 8 world heritage sites in Sri Lanka. What is stopping such an investment – safety. While no one has got killed in recent times in Sri Lanka due to train accidents, the railway records show many derailments caused by poor maintenance. 

2.My second moonshot is even more ambitious: to explore the possibility of bringing Formula 1 to Colombo following the successful example of Singapore. F1 wants to be in South Asia, but was discontinued in India after 2013 following commercial, tax and regulatory difficulties. We have a perfect track in Colombo stretching from Port City to Galle Face and Baladaksha Mawatha. We also have superior logistics. This would undoubtedly be a complex undertaking, requiring substantial investment, Government coordination and a long-term commercial commitment. But we should at least explore the opportunity, considering there is potential investment interest from India.

Conclusion: Time to realise our potential

Let me conclude by returning to the question of value. A good friend of mine, Navjit Ahluwalia, who is now with Mandarin Oriental, made a statement that has resonated with me: “Before COVID, $1,000 a night was a ceiling for a great resort. Today it is the floor.” He was referring to the growth of the ultra-luxury market and the ability of truly distinctive properties to command extraordinary rates.

The underlying point is that the value of a luxury experience increasingly depends on its rarity. The world’s most discerning travellers are prepared to pay a premium for properties that offer something they cannot easily find elsewhere. This principle has influenced my own work over the past several years, including the investments I pursue, the projects on which my company advises, and the boards on which I serve.

Sri Lanka has a significant opportunity in this segment. It has been 27 years since the Aman brand established a presence in Sri Lanka. We should ask why the country has not attracted more internationally recognised ultra-luxury resorts in the intervening period.

I am however pleased to say that management agreements have recently been signed for a Ritz-Carlton Reserve resort project in Sri Lanka, which is proceeding through its preliminary approvals. There is also interest from other international hospitality brands, supported by investments from India and the Middle East. These developments are encouraging. They suggest that, despite the policy missteps of the past, a new wave of international investments and brands could still reshape Sri Lanka’s resort landscape.

Sri Lanka has been blessed with extraordinary natural and cultural assets. What we have lacked is a consistent strategy for converting our assets into sustainable economic value. We must move beyond the assumption that more hotel rooms and more tourist arrivals will automatically deliver success.
